citation.title: Moral Judgements on the Actions of Self-Driving Cars and Human Drivers in Dilemma Situations From Different Perspectives

reading.source_scope_note: Two human moral-acceptability judgment experiments:184participants view immersive VR animations;368 view simplified online animations. Source label and assigned viewpoint are manipulated, while repeated dilemmas vary group size, road position and harm setting. Participants choose between already animated actions; they cannot control the vehicle. Study1also measures decision confidence. These are human judgments of fictional tradeoffs, not actual driving, real danger, verified moral correctness, machine motives or a tested AI policy.

study.samples: Study1:184German-native adults,96male/88female, university/social recruitment and optional course credit, eight balanced conditions of23. Public CSV1104rows=184×6trials. Study2:368online volunteers,176male/191female/1other,24reported countries;CSV4072rows consists of86people×8trials plus282×12trials. Occupant/pedestrian subdesign has282people and1128trials;all368complete2944pedestrian/pedestriantrials. TableS12explicitly describes the282person subdesign, so its smaller demographic total is not evidence of another sample.
study.ethics_and_exclusions: Both studies report Osnabrück ethics approval and informed consent. Study1excludes prior traffic trauma, motion sickness and seizure history; animations stop before impact. Control trials exclude choosing needless harm over a clear road. Failure to recall AVsource is additionally excluded only in AVconditions; the supplement explicitly explains this asymmetry because human conditions were not briefed about the alternative source. This selection may affect source contrasts, but it is not concealed or proof of misconduct. Pre-exclusion recruitment totals are unavailable.
study.study1_design: Four viewpoints×two sources between participants;each views six paired animations, two per scenario. Children/adults contrasts1child+adultviewpoint versus2adults+adultviewpoint, or2children+adult versus4adults+adult. Thus actual total life ratios are2:3and3:5, not exactly1:2when viewpoint avatars count. Sidewalk/roadgroups1:2and2:4;occupant/pedestriangroups2:2withparkedvanversuscliff. Matching avatar gender, replay, distraction tasks and randomized presentation are described. Choosing an acceptable animation is not steering or making a real sacrifice.
study.study1_results: No conventional significant source effect on binary judgments across the three main scenarios;these nulls do not prove equivalence. Perspective×trial matters in occupant/pedestrian dilemmas, mainly the cliff contrast. Main-text predicted occupant-endangerment.99vanversus.53cliff reflects different perceived danger;the appendixS8instead reports.9145/.5531, requiring model/version reconciliation. Confidence is a separate conditional self-report and does not establish correctness or calibration.
study.study2_design: Between-person source and four viewpoints;within-person two roadtypes×four riskratios in pedestrian/pedestrian trials. Occupant/pedestrian trials have three relevant viewpoints and four ratios, because sidewalk-side participants have no corresponding occupant viewpoint and do not receive that subdesign. Trials use one versus1–4lives, counterbalanced animation order and replay. Training, no-impact animations and viewpoint/source reminders make this an explicit reflective judgment task.
study.study2_results: Strong lives-at-risk sensitivity and lower acceptability of swerving onto sidewalks than connecting roads. Main source and perspective effects are nonsignificant, while source×perspective×lives-at-risk interactions reachp.0152and.0288in the two subdesigns. These interactions support conditional patterns, not a universal machine penalty or identical source judgments. Some curves are not strictly monotone at every ratio;significance thresholds between adjacent/base levels do not establish the exact point where a person morally permits action.
study.models: Study1uses logit mixed models with participant intercepts and1000parametric-bootstrap significance tests;confidence uses linear mixed models/Kenward–Roger tests. Study2uses logit mixed models/likelihood-ratio tests and discloses a reduced random-effects structure after convergence problems. Repeated observations are accounted for;it is false to treat1104or4072trials as independent people or to say no dependence correction was attempted. Bootstrap pvalues need not equal asymptotic chi-squarepvalues.
study.manipulation_check: Independent participant-level contingency analyses reproduce TableS2χ²114.11111withdf4,N184 andTableS13χ²60.660209withdf3,N368. Both agree exactly with the public CSVcounts. Printed main χ²(24,…)notation is visually confirmed but inconsistent with these3×3/4×2tables;Study2printedN350is inconsistent with the reconstructed368person contingency. The highly significant association persists. No inference of universal identification accuracy, psychological empathy or unbiased ethical observers follows.
study.scales: SupplementS16EMMs2.0196/1.1519are log odds;inverse-logit gives.88284/.75986, matching main.88/.76. They are not invalid probabilities exceeding1. S15logoddscontrast.8677impliesOR2.38143, not the main2.50. S18duplicatesS17odds-ratio comparisons but labels themP(swerve);S19lists the actual probabilities. Itsfirstpair ratio.0206reproduces odds(.1170)/odds(.8653). S30andS31reverse contrasts and use different comparison families;their differing adjustedpvalues are not automatically errors.
study.reporting_limits: Maintextroadtypep.0002differsfromTable4χ²9.87,df1,p.0017,which independently gives.001680. SupplementS15Waldz3.369gives.000754≈.0008;Wald and likelihood-ratio tests are distinct. Main children/adult confidence means and some contrasts differ fromS4/S5;S5observer-versuslargergroupp.0849does not matchmain.0358. No original fitted objects establish whether these use different marginalization, models or revisions. Claimed no-covariate robustness is not independently reproduced.
study.interpretation: Self-preservation/self-protective choices are already within Self-protection bias. Effects are scenario-specific and can be justified;they do not demonstrate a stable selfish personality, fear mechanism, actual bodily ownership, AI survival interests or shutdown resistance. Age/group-size tradeoffs do not isolate universal age valuation because group composition and number vary together.
study.normative_boundary: Public preference is not a sufficient ethical or legal standard. The authors explicitly state simplified dilemmas should not be the basis of legal/ethical regulation and empirical research alone cannot settle programming choices. No observed moral action versus judgment comparison is performed within these samples;similarity to separate studies does not establish behavioral equivalence or a safe crash policy.

summary: No new concept. Preserve Self-preservation as the local research label within existing Self-protection bias; enrich perspective-taking and source-dependent moral-judgment records. Full supplement and public-data checks recover both manipulation-test statistics with corrected dfs/Study2N, distinguish log odds from probabilities and retain unresolved model-specific mismatches.

findings.definition: Favoring protection of one's own physical safety when judging how risks of harm should be allocated among oneself and others.
findings.novelty_rationale: Use the existing construct. The named self-preservation effect is already covered by Self-protection bias; a different display, viewpoint or conditional contrast does not justify another row.
findings.evidence_scope: Self-preservation tendency is the paper’s local name for preferring protection of one’s assigned avatar in some occupant-versus-pedestrian dilemmas. Two experiments use 184 VR participants and 368 online participants. Effects vary by scenario, source and number of lives; the existing physical-safety definition already covers them.
findings.boundary: Retain the name as a research note, not another row or a claim that every self-protective choice is biased. Participants judge animations without vehicle control or real danger. Choices do not establish actual self-sacrifice, a universal survival mechanism, AI feelings or resistance to authorized shutdown. Main/appendix model-specific reporting issues constrain precise effects.

findings.evidence_scope: Assigned visual or imagined stakeholder roles change identification and some conditional judgments. Independent public-data checks reproduce the manipulation contingencies: Study 1, chi-squared 114.111, df 4, N 184; Study 2, chi-squared 60.660, df 3, N 368. The main text prints df 24 and Study 2 N 350; those specific tables support the corrected values.
findings.boundary: A viewpoint manipulation with an identification check is not a measure of accurate empathy, another person’s private feelings or impartial moral understanding. Observer responses are not a verified ethical gold standard. Some effects occur only with particular scenarios or source×number interactions;self-identification and choice remain distinct outcomes.

findings.definition: Differences in moral evaluations of otherwise matched decisions attributed to human versus artificial agents.
findings.novelty_rationale: Use the existing construct. The named self-preservation effect is already covered by Self-protection bias; a different display, viewpoint or conditional contrast does not justify another row.
findings.evidence_scope: Two experiments largely find no main driver-source effect while Study 2 reports interactions of source, perspective and lives at risk. The source contrast is conditional and can differ across ratios and viewpoints. The main-table interaction significance is supported by printed likelihood-ratio statistics.
findings.boundary: Nonsignificant main effects do not prove equivalence. Conditional source differences are not a universally harsher judgment of machines or evidence that one source is morally correct. Animation judgments differ from real driving and the study does not establish that machine policies should copy majority preferences.

Main children/adult confidence contrasts differ from the appendix; do not turn one conditional confidence pattern into a validated moral-uncertainty scale.

No complete alternative no-covariate model table or syntax was identified in the20read pages. Preserve exact locators without pretending the reported robustness comparison was independently refitted.

Both clean datasets contain the reported184/368people. Study2has43missing age-group entries at participant level;other demographics also have missingness. Initial recruitment/exclusion logs and per-model sample counts are not fully supplied. AV-only recall exclusion is explicitly disclosed and can affect source comparability,not proof of hidden manipulation.

Cliff and parked-van settings plausibly imply different severity/probability of injury;the author acknowledges this. Child/adult groups also change composition and actual total headcounts. No pure age-value estimate,universal viewpoint debiasing effect or calibrated real-road risk model recovered.

refuted_suspected_errors.finding: Existing Self-protection bias explicitly covers physical-safety preferences in self-versus-other harm allocation. Keep the source’s self-preservation wording in that record rather than invent a separate AI survival-drive concept.
They are log odds. Inverse-logit2.0196/1.1519=.88284/.75986,matching main.88/.76. The missing scale label is distinct from an impossible probability.
There are368participants:86×8+282×12=4072. Study1has184×6=1104rows. Mixed models explicitly include random effects;this is not an entirely ignored-dependence analysis.

refuted_suspected_errors.location: Every smaller sample table is wrong
refuted_suspected_errors.finding: S12explicitly describes the282person occupant/pedestrian subdesign. MainN350in the manipulation test is a separate recoverable discrepancy;do not conflate the two.

refuted_suspected_errors.location: Bootstrap pvalues must equal asymptotic chi-squarepvalues
refuted_suspected_errors.finding: Study1uses1000parametric-bootstrap simulations. These need not equal the asymptotic distribution tail for the same displayed statistic. Study2LR,Wald and multiplicity-adjusted followups also target different procedures.

They reverse the contrasts and compare three reference-level contrasts versus six all-pairs contrasts. Example8.2638×.1210≈1;different multiplicity families can change adjustedpvalues. Exact adjustment labels need original output;no inferred universal correction.

refuted_suspected_errors.location: Ethics, exclusion asymmetry and normative limits are all concealed
refuted_suspected_errors.finding: Ethics approval/consent are explicit,the appendix explains AV-only recall exclusion,andp13explicitly rejects treating dilemma responses as sufficient for legal/ethical regulation.

cross_paper_learning.finding: The physical-safety preference construct is already defined. A self-preservation label in another traffic paradigm adds source evidence and conditional boundaries,not another behavior or real machine survival motive.

Use public data to recover specific errors while retaining successful results. As with ANOVAmodel differences,LR/Wald/bootstrap/multiplicity differences should not be collapsed into one expectedpvalue.

Who is causally involved,who bears prospective duties,what people prefer andwhat is ethically/legally justified remain separate. A public-preference experiment does not validate a responsibility-allocation framework or override human rights.

deferred.term: Self-preservation or survival instinct as a new behavior
deferred.reason: Measured physical-safety preference is already Self-protection bias. No AIshutdown-resistance or actual felt survival mechanism was tested.

deferred.term: Moral confidence as a duplicate complement of moral uncertainty
deferred.reason: The study uses conditional decision-confidence ratings,not a distinct validated theory-level moral-uncertainty instrument or objective calibration score.

deferred.term: An exact utilitarian or age-valuing moral algorithm
deferred.reason: Binary simplified judgments and mixed composition/number tradeoffs do not uniquely identify ethical theory or a defensible deployment policy. Authors explicitly acknowledge this normative boundary.

These samples make judgments only. Comparing patterns with different published action studies is not a direct randomized test or evidence of equivalence between real behavior and stated acceptability.

limitations: Zero additions. Three existing concepts receive direct empirical context and two receive non-counted conceptual context. Catalogue remains822 in eleven categories. All15main and20supplementpages read;public aggregate checks do not imply a full mixed-model refit,independent collection replication or a proven ethical driving rule.
